newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Market manipulation hard to define - Hong Kong SFC.
newsitem.headline: Market manipulation hard to define - Hong Kong SFC.

text.p: Volatile trading in the Hong Kong stock market last Thursday has led to an examination of the day's trades by the stock exchange, but regulatory authorities said it would be difficult to prove a false market was created.

"There is a fine line between legitimate hedging operations, legitimate trading strategies and market manipulation," Gerard McMahon, executive director of the Securities and Futures Commission, said on Wednesday.
"We have to determine whether in any particular case that line has been crossed."
The stock exchange said last Thursday it was examining the opening transactions in a number of stocks and asking the brokers involved to explain the trades.
The Hang Seng Index swung through 444 points last Thursday, leaping 213 points to an all-time high of 13,744.30 in the first 15 minutes of trade before ending 220.19 points down at 13,310.76.
Thursday also was the last day for trading in the November Hang Seng Index futures contract.
"It is not going to be a case in which we are going to come out with a quick solution because we are going to interview the people involved and find out their side of the story," said McMahon.
"Market manipulation is notoriously worldwide a difficult thing to define."
Section 135 of Hong Kong's Securities Ordinance prohibits the creation of a false market or false trading, he said.
"It is necessary for us to be satisfied what occurred was not motivated by the desire to create a false market and the way in which it was done," he said.

Speaking on whether authorities should take criminal or civil action against those believed to have committed market abuses, McMahon said the main thing was to make sure that abuses were exposed quickly and that penalties were meaningful.
"When it comes to a big market intermediary we all know that market confidence is a huge factor," he said.
"If investors lose confidence because of the exposure of a market abuse which has been carried out by an intermediary that in itself is a very, very significant penalty."
McMahon said Hong Kong did not need more regulation but that authorities should continue to be more effective in implementing existing rules.
